newsitem.title: PERU: Japanese-Peruvians fear a backlash from the siege.
newsitem.headline: Japanese-Peruvians fear a backlash from the siege.

text.p: Caught between two cultures, Peruvians of Japanese descent worry increasingly about a backlash from both Japan and Peru because of the hostage siege at the Japan ambassador's residence.
Some fear they are about to pay for the sudden rise from obscurity of President Alberto Fujimori, the son of a tailor who emigrated from a Japanese village to Peru early this century.
Fujimori was elected in 1990 as leader of a nation where those of Spanish ancestry were always the aristocrats.

"It depends on the outcome (of the crisis)," Ricardo Higa, an editor at the bilingual daily Peru Shimpo, said. "If Fujimori does something that angers the nation, then there might be another backlash."
They worry that despite Fujimori's recent political success, the community has a history mainly of being victims rather than an elite group.

Older people still remember angry mobs tearing through Lima in May 1940, when Japanese-Peruvian businesses were ransacked. When Japan bombed Pearl Harbour, about 1,400 Japanese-Peruvians were deported to be interned in camps in the United States.

Some "nikkei," or Japanese-Peruvians, say they sense a a feeling that they are somehow to blame for the embarrassment of both their ancestral and adopted homes caused by the hostage crisis in the residence of the Japanese envoy.

In the week since the Marxist Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stormed the Japanese embassy residence, the 80,000-strong Japanese-Peruvian community has retreated into reflective anonymity after an initial willingness to share the drama and their lives.

They say the spotlight cast on them by the hordes of news people who have descended on Peru may mistakenly portray the Andean nation as a "Little Tokyo," a land of sushi bars, Buddhist temples and rich businessmen who rule the roost over the Indians and Spanish settlers.
In fact, the Japanese community is a tiny minority among the 24 million Peruvians, who are mostly of Inca Indian descent, though Japanese and Indians share some physical similarities.

"Look in the Lima telephone book. There are only five Japanese restaraunts listed. Yet there are 50 Chinese and 16 Italian restaraunts," one nikkei man said. "Most of us could never afford to eat Japanese food every day."
At Fuji, one of the five restaurants, the owner and the sushi chef, along with several Japanese regulars, watched the latest developments in the hostage crisis.
The owner, a Japanese, said he employeed only Japanese or Peruvians, not nikkei. "Nikkei are not really Japanese. I find them to be more Peruvian than Peruvians," he said.

"Most Japanese people are a little bit cold to us," said Carlos Ujiike, a third-generation nikkei journalist who spent two years studying in Japan. "When Fujimori was elected, they seemed to give us more respect, but I can't predict if that would change if he was to be succeeded by a Peruvian."
Ujiike works in the simple, wood-panelled office of Peru Shimpo, which is delivered to nikkei homes in Lima.
The first 790 Japanese immmigrants arrived in Peru in 1899 and became farmers, though many later moved to the cities to take up jobs in commerce and industry.
Many families now include successful shop owners, doctors and engineers, but it was not until Fujimori's rise to power that nikkei began to hold prominent positions in government.
The current administration has three nikkei Cabinet ministers, including the speaker of Congress, Jaime Yoshiyama.
"The best thing that has happened (since Fujimori took office) is that our children now have pride," Claudia Takata, a third-generation nikkei secretary, said.

Things were not always so good. Like the Indians before them, Japanese-Peruvians were subject to racist discrimination several times this century, most strongly during the Second World War, when Peru's government took the side of the Allies against the Axis powers of Germany and Japan.

When Fujimori became the surprise favourite to win the presidency in 1990, a wave of anti-Asian sentiment swept the capital, from insults hurled on the streets to the reported stoning of some Japanese-Peruvian homes.
Some nikkei, buckling under the economic hardships of the rampant inflation of the late 1980s and early 1990s, returned to their ancestral homeland as temporary manual labourers.
Jesus Omote, a third-generation nikkei who worked in Japan for five years, returned last year to drive a taxi in Lima. "It's a beautiful country, but I couldn't really fit in there," he said.
